Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation
lectures.title: Blood Pressure Regulation, PHE Screening and the Mental Health Screen
lectures.framing: Three strands from one week: what to screen for at a periodic health encounter, how BP is set (MAP = CO × TPR, adjusted fast by the ANS and slowly by hormones), and how to screen for mental illness. The organising idea for BP is that every regulator acts on either CO or TPR.
lectures.keypoints: Annual physicals do not improve outcomes; PHE screening is risk-factor driven. MAP = DP + 1/3 (SP - DP) = CO × TPR, and CO = HR × SV. The PNS does not innervate blood vessels; vascular tone is set by changing tonic SNS firing. AC/BD: α constricts, β2 dilates. Anxiety needs ~6 months of symptoms, depression ~2 weeks.

blocks.html:

blocks.html:
Blood pressure
  • Blood pressure (BP): pressure exerted by blood on the walls of the blood vessels; means arterial pressure in the systemic circulation
  • BP = systolic / diastolic = 120/80 mmHg
  • R side = pulmonary circulation (CO2-rich, O2-poor blood); L side = systemic circulation (O2-rich, CO2-poor blood)
  • Total blood volume ≈ 5 L: heart + pulmonary circulation 15%, systemic arteries (distribution vessels) 10%, systemic capillaries (exchange vessels) 5%, systemic veins (capacitance vessels) 70%

blocks.cap: Pressure falls most steeply across the arterioles (the resistance vessels); by the capillaries and veins it is low and non-pulsatile.

blocks.html:
• Risk categories: low = 120/80; medium = 121-139/80-89; high = ≥ 140/90
  • Physiological factors: age, gender, genetics, diet, sleep, activity, stress, hydration
  • Circulatory factors: cardiac output (heart) and peripheral resistance (blood vessels)

Mean arterial pressure (MAP)
  • MAP: average BP over a single cardiac cycle
    MAP = DP + 1/3 (SP - DP) ≈ 93 mmHg
    MAP = CO × TPR
  • Cardiac output (CO): blood ejected by the heart in one minute (L/min); CO = HR × SV
  • Heart rate (HR): contractions per minute
  • Stroke volume (SV): blood ejected in one contraction
  • Total peripheral resistance (TPR): total resistance the blood meets from all the blood vessels

Blood pressure regulation
  • Autonomic nervous system: short-term, rapid response; controls visceral (involuntary) functions
  • Hormonal mechanisms: long-term, slow response

Causes both vasoconstriction and vasodilation by changing its tonic activity to the arterioles

lectures.name: Body Systems Integration
lectures.title: Body System Integration
lectures.framing: How the circulation ties every organ system together: each system section traces where the blood (or lymph) arrives, what is exchanged, and where it drains.
lectures.keypoints: Tunica media is thicker in arteries because of higher pressure. Coronary arteries take 5% of CO and drain via the coronary sinus to the RA. The thoracic duct drains ¾ of the body into the L subclavian/IJ; the R lymphatic duct drains the R upper quadrant. Gut venous blood passes the liver via the portal system before the IVC. RBCs live 100-120 days, cleared by splenic red pulp.

blocks.html:
Cardiovascular: the vessel wall
  • Tunica intima (innermost): simple squamous endothelium, in direct contact with blood in the lumen
  • Tunica media (middle): circular smooth muscle; contraction = vasoconstriction, relaxation = vasodilation; thicker in arteries because of ↑ BP
  • Tunica externa (outermost): connective tissue; protects and strengthens the wall
  • Capillaries: RBCs pass in single file; renew surrounding tissue fluid; deliver O2/nutrients, remove CO2/wastes

Respiratory: pulmonary circulation
  • RBCs carry CO2 back to the heart via the superior/inferior venae cavae → R atrium → R ventricle → pulmonary arteries → lungs → alveoli
  • Respiration moves O2 from bronchial tree to RBC (inspiration) and CO2 from RBC to bronchial tree (expiration)
  • Oxygenated blood returns via the pulmonary veins → L atrium, ready for the systemic circulation

flowchart LR A["Superior and inferior
venae cavae
CO2-rich blood"] --> B["R atrium"] --> C["R ventricle"] --> D["Pulmonary arteries"] --> E["Lungs and alveoli
O2 in, CO2 out"] --> F["Pulmonary veins"] --> G["L atrium"] --> H["Systemic circulation"]

blocks.html:
Coronary circulation
  • The heart supplies itself with oxygenated blood before sending it to the rest of the body
  • Coronary arteries (5% of CO) → heart muscle → coronary veins → coronary sinus → R atrium
  • Occlusion of coronary arteries by atherosclerosis can cause a myocardial infarction
Musculoskeletal
  • Oxygenated RBCs travel through the systemic arterial tree to working muscle; O2/CO2 exchange
  • Deoxygenated RBCs return through the venous system → R atrium
  • Wastes of muscle metabolism are processed in the liver once they reach it via the systemic circulation

Lymphatic
  • Lymphatic vessels collect excess fluid (water, ions, nutrient molecules, respiratory gases) from the areolar connective tissue around blood capillaries and return it (as lymph) to the bloodstream
  • Maintains blood volume: returns leaked proteins to the systemic circulation
  • Thoracic duct → L subclavian / internal jugular vein: drains ¾ of the body (L head/neck/thorax/upper limb + the whole lower body)
  • R lymphatic duct → R subclavian / internal jugular vein: drains the R upper quadrant (R head/neck/thorax/upper limb)
  • Any blockage of lymphatic vessels → the region swells with excess tissue fluid (edema)

blocks.html:
Gastrointestinal
  • Oxygenated blood reaches the GI tract via the abdominal aorta
  • Absorbed nutrients → venous system → portal system → liver → caval system → IVC → R atrium
Urinary
  • Oxygenated blood reaches the kidney via the renal arteries → nephron
  • Renal corpuscle: glomerulus → glomerular capsule
  • Renal tubule: PCT → loop of Henle → DCT → collecting duct → ureter → bladder
  • Peritubular capillaries surround the tubule and reabsorb water/ions/nutrients into the blood → venous circulation
Endocrine
  • Oxygenated blood reaches each endocrine organ through the systemic circulation
  • Endocrine cells release hormones into the surrounding extracellular space → capillaries → venous system → target organ
RBC end of life
  • RBCs live 100-120 days in the circulation of a healthy person
  • The spleen removes and destroys aged/defective blood cells (red pulp: macrophages) and blood-borne antigens (white pulp: immune function)

lectures.name: Introduction to the Nervous System
lectures.title: Introduction to the Nervous System
lectures.framing: The peripheral nervous system as a set of routes: somatic sensory in and motor out, the sympathetic chain (thoracolumbar, short pre / long post) and the parasympathetic outflow (craniosacral, long pre / short post). Referred pain follows the same wiring back to the cord.
lectures.keypoints: WRC only at T1-L2/3; GRC on every spinal nerve. Abdominopelvic viscera: pre-synaptic fibres pass through the chain without synapsing as splanchnic nerves (T5-L2/3). Patellar and Achilles reflexes are monosynaptic. No parasympathetics to skin or limbs. Visceral pain is referred to the body wall of the cord levels its afferents enter: follow sympathetics to T1-L3, parasympathetics to S2-4.

blocks.html:
Organization
  • CNS: brain, spinal cord
  • PNS: 12 cranial nerve pairs + 31 spinal nerve pairs (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal)
  • Sensory = afferent; motor = efferent
Somatic nervous system
  • Conveyed by all spinal nerves and 4 cranial nerves
  • General sensory fibres: carry sensation from the body wall (skin, skeletal muscle, joints) to the CNS: pain, proprioception, temperature, pressure, touch
  • General motor fibres: carry impulses to skeletal muscle

blocks.cap: Generic spinal nerve: sensory (blue) enters via the DRG and dorsal root; motor (red) leaves via the ventral root. Dorsal rami supply the back, ventral rami the limbs and rest of the trunk.

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["General sensory neuron
receptor"] --> B["Ramus"] --> C["Spinal nerve"] --> D["DRG"] --> E["Dorsal root"] --> F["Dorsal grey horn"] F -->|"Somatic pathway"| G["Secondary neuron to brain"] G --> H["UMN to ventral grey horn"] F -->|"Reflex arc"| I["Interneuron
polysynaptic"] I --> J["Ventral grey horn"] H --> K["LMN = general motor neuron"] J --> K K --> M["Ventral root"] --> N["Spinal nerve"] --> O["Ramus to muscle"]

blocks.html:
• Somatic pathway: sensory neuron up to the brain, UMN back down to the ventral horn, LMN out to muscle
  • Reflex arc: an interneuron in the cord links sensory to motor (polysynaptic)
  • Patellar and Achilles reflexes have no interneuron (monosynaptic)

Autonomic nervous system
  • Visceral motor nerves: act on viscera, smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands
Sympathetic (thoracolumbar)
  • Fight or flight: dilates pupils, ↑ HR/contractility, dilates bronchioles, dilates vessels to skeletal muscle, constricts vessels to GI organs, ↓ GI peristalsis, activates sweat secretion
  • Pre-synaptic neuron (short): cell body in the intermediolateral grey horn; enters the chain via the white ramus communicans (WRC), present only at T1-L2/3
  • Sympathetic chain: row of paravertebral ganglia running bilaterally along the vertebral column
  • Post-synaptic neuron (long): cell body in a chain ganglion; leaves via the grey ramus communicans (GRC), present on all spinal nerves
  • Cervical region has only superior, middle and inferior ganglia; the inferior often fuses with T1 to form the stellate ganglion

blocks.cap: Pre-synaptic fibre (green) enters the chain through the WRC and synapses; the post-synaptic fibre (blue) rejoins the spinal nerve through the GRC. Only T1-L2/3 have a WRC; every level has a GRC.

blocks.html:
• Levels for head and limbs: head = superior cervical ganglion, upper limb = cervical ganglia, lower limb = L2-S3
  • Abdominopelvic route: pre-synaptic fibre is long, post-synaptic short (reverse of the usual); the notes call the outside ganglion "paravertebral ganglion outside the sympathetic chain"

Parasympathetic (craniosacral)
  • No parasympathetic component in spinal nerves, so no parasympathetic input to skin or extremities
  • Rest and digest: lacrimation, salivation, urination, digestion, defecation, sexual arousal
  • Pre-synaptic neuron long → synapse in ganglia close to the target → post-synaptic neuron short

rows: Pre-synaptic neuron from CNS nuclei → parasympathetic ganglion (ciliary, pterygopalatine, otic, submandibular) → post-synaptic neuron travels with CN V to the target

blocks.html:
General visceral afferents and referred pain
  • Embryonically each spinal nerve supplies one patch of skin (dermatome) and muscle (myotome); as the embryo elongates the patches converge, mixing the nerve supply
  • Visceral afferent route: visceral sensory neuron → thoracoabdominal splanchnic nerve → sympathetic chain → WRC → spinal nerve → DRG → dorsal root → dorsal grey horn → second-order neuron → brain
  • Referred pain: the brain is used to receiving body-wall sensation at those cord levels, so it misreads visceral pain as body-wall pain of the same spinal levels; diffuse, non-specific, achy
  • Pelvic pain line = lower limit of the peritoneum
  • Visceral pain: follow sympathetics to T1-L3 spinal levels; follow parasympathetics to S2-4 spinal levels

lectures.name: Cellular Stress & Repair
lectures.title: Cell Regeneration and Repair
lectures.framing: After injury, tissue either regenerates (normal function restored) or is repaired by scar. Which one happens depends on how severe the injury is and whether the cells can divide.
lectures.keypoints: Labile and stable cells regenerate; permanent cells always scar (cardiac myocytes, neurons, skeletal muscle cells, RBCs). Scar formation runs angiogenesis → granulation tissue → remodelling. A scar gives stability but the tissue never functions normally again. Repair is impaired by infection, diabetes, poor nutrition (vitamin C), glucocorticoids, mechanical stress, poor blood supply and foreign bodies.

rows: Severe: tissue lacks regenerative capacity, or supporting structures are badly damaged

Labile (continuously dividing) and stable cells
Occurs constantly in skin and GI epithelium, and after injury in cells in G0
Permanent cells cannot regenerate and always heal by scarring: cardiac myocytes, neurons, skeletal muscle cells, RBCs

Proliferation of uninjured cells and/or maturation of tissue stem cells
Macrophages, epithelial and stromal cells release growth factors → bind ECM proteins; ↑ protein production drives cells through the cycle and releases checkpoint blocks
Quiescent tissue stem cells proliferate → differentiate into mature cells

1. Angiogenesis: new blood vessels
2. Granulation tissue: thin-walled capillaries, leukocytes, loose connective tissue (ECM), proliferating fibroblasts
3. Connective tissue remodelling: maturation/organization into a stable fibrous scar
Stability, perhaps some return of function, but the tissue never functions normally again

Factors that influence repair
  • Infection
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Nutritional status (vitamin C deficiency)
  • Glucocorticoids (steroids)
  • Mechanical factors (pressure, torsion)
  • Poor blood supply
  • Foreign bodies
  • Type, extent and location of injury

lectures.name: Adult Screening - Diagnostic Pathway
lectures.title: Adult Screening: the Diagnostic Pathway and Lab Test Performance
lectures.framing: A PHE for a young, healthy adult is risk-factor driven, not a fixed panel. The rest of the lecture is the toolkit for judging any test: where the decision threshold sits, and how sensitivity, specificity and predictive values trade against each other.
lectures.keypoints: SPIN / SNOUT: a specific positive rules in, a sensitive negative rules out. Lowering a cut-point ↑ sensitivity, ↓ specificity. Screen with a very sensitive test, confirm with a very specific one. PPV and NPV change with prevalence; higher pretest probability = higher PPV. A reference interval is the central 95% of a healthy population (> 120 per partition to establish, > 20 to verify).

Substance misuse: "How much alcohol do you drink in a week?" "Do you use any other drugs?"

blocks.html:
Lab test performance
  • Accuracy: how well the data match the true value
  • Precision: how close the data are to each other (spread)
  • Decision threshold: cut-off at the upper limit of the reference range
  • Disease absent: below threshold = true negative (TN); above = false positive (FP)
  • Disease present: below = false negative (FN); above = true positive (TP)

blocks.cap: Moving the threshold left catches more disease (↑ sensitivity) at the cost of more false positives; moving it right does the reverse (↑ specificity).

rows: % probability that a positive result correctly predicts presence of disease
% probability that a negative result correctly predicts absence of disease

blocks.lead: The 2 × 2 table (example: a test with 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity)

blocks.html:
Screening
  • Screening tests are done routinely, at set intervals, on asymptomatic patients for early detection
  • Lowering a screening cut-point ↑ sensitivity but ↓ specificity: SPIN, SNOUT
  • Use a very sensitive test in the asymptomatic population, then a very specific test for diagnosis
  • Consider the extra clinical benefit/cost of screening-informed management, value for money, and consequences
  • Prevalence: % of tested patients who have the disease; predictive values change with prevalence
  • Pretest probability: likelihood the patient has the disease; higher pretest probability = higher PPV
  • ROC curve: false positive rate (x-axis, 1 - specificity) vs. true positive rate (y-axis, sensitivity); larger area under the curve = more effective test

lectures.name: Choosing Wisely Review
lectures.title: Choosing Wisely
lectures.framing: More is not always better. Choosing Wisely is about appropriate test use: avoiding overuse without sliding into underuse.
lectures.keypoints: Inappropriate testing causes unnecessary procedures, treatment and patient harm, and adds cost to the system. The recommendations (348) are evidence-based and made by multidisciplinary stakeholders, for clinicians and patients alike. Overuse has drivers at every level: labs, systems, physicians (malpractice fear, fee for service) and patients ("more is better", Dr. Google).

blocks.html:
• More is not always better
  • Choosing Wisely = appropriate utilization of tests, balancing underutilization and overutilization
  • Inappropriate utilization → unnecessary procedures and treatment → inappropriate care or patient harm
  • Inappropriate utilization → ↑ cost burden to the health care system
  • Recommendations are evidence-based and generated by multidisciplinary stakeholders
  • 348 recommendations, for clinicians and patients to make informed decisions about care
  • Tool kits are available to implement Choosing Wisely in practice

lectures.name: Approach to Anxiety and Stress
lectures.title: Effects of Stress and Inflammation on Blood Vessels
lectures.framing: Stressors (infection, AGEs, hemodynamic stress, lipids, hypoxia) activate the endothelium; the vessel's response is repair with intimal thickening, which is the common root of hypertension damage and atherosclerosis.
lectures.keypoints: Normal endothelium is non-thrombogenic and controls tone (NO relaxes, endothelin contracts). Intimal thickening → stenosis, obstruction, ↓ organ blood flow. AGEs matter in diabetes; hemodynamic stress and lipids in atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis starts with endothelial dysfunction, then lipoprotein entry, monocyte → macrophage → foam cell, platelets, smooth muscle recruitment and proliferation, ECM, T cells, lipid accumulation.

rows:
Non-thrombogenic surface
Modulate tone and control growth of smooth muscle cells

Express adhesion molecules
Produce cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, vasoactive molecules (vasoconstriction or vasodilation), procoagulant and anticoagulant factors
Affect vasoreactivity of underlying smooth muscle: relaxing factor = nitric oxide; contracting factor = endothelin

blocks.html:
What activates endothelium
  • Infection and inflammation: viruses, bacterial products, complement, cytokines
  • Advanced glycation end-products: important in the pathologic sequelae of diabetes
  • Hemodynamic stresses and lipid products: critical to the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis
  • Hypoxia: oxygen deprivation
Response to injury
  • Vascular damage/dysfunction → repair similar to other tissues, with intimal thickening
  • Intimal thickening → luminal stenosis, vascular obstruction, ↓ blood flow to an organ/tissue

blocks.cap: Intimal thickening: smooth muscle cells are recruited from the media into the intima, divide, and lay down extracellular matrix beneath the endothelium.

blocks.html:
Hypertension
  • Elevated blood pressure → hemodynamic stress, which may ↑ endothelial injury or dysfunction
  • Complications: atherosclerosis (myocardial infarction), cardiac hypertrophy/heart failure, multi-infarct dementia, aortic dissection, cerebrovascular hemorrhage, renal failure
Atherosclerosis
  • Thickening or hardening of the arteries; a sequence of events believed to be a response to endothelial dysfunction (sometimes endothelial injury)
  • Causes: hemodynamic disturbance, hypercholesterolemia
  • Complications: thrombosis and vessel occlusion, hemorrhage into plaque, atheroembolism, aneurysm formation
  • Consequences: myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction (stroke), aortic aneurysm, peripheral vascular disease
Sequence of atherogenesis
  1. Endothelial dysfunction → ↑ vascular permeability, leukocyte adhesion, thrombosis
  2. Lipoproteins accumulate in the vessel wall
  3. Monocytes adhere, migrate into the intima, become macrophages and foam cells
  4. Platelets adhere to the endothelium
  5. Activated platelets, macrophages and vascular wall cells release factors → smooth muscle recruitment
  6. Smooth muscle cells proliferate
  7. Extracellular matrix is produced
  8. T cells are recruited
  9. Lipids accumulate extracellularly and within cells (macrophages and smooth muscle cells)

lectures.name: Approach to Abnormal Test Results
lectures.title: Approach to Abnormal Test Results; Dehydration and RAAS
lectures.framing: Two approaches in one lecture: a seven-step routine for an unexpected lab value (check pre-analytical, analytical and post-analytical error before believing it), and the body's own response to low volume: ADH, thirst and RAAS.
lectures.keypoints: Unexpected result: work through pre-analytical → analytical → post-analytical explanations, talk to the lab, retest, and remember the result may be correct. Dehydration: ADH conserves water, thirst restores volume. RAAS is triggered by ↓ BP and ↑ extracellular K+ and inhibited by ANP and BNP. Angiotensin II → aldosterone (↑ Na+ reabsorption), vasoconstriction, ADH/thirst → ↑ ECF and BP.

blocks.html:
Approach to an unexpected lab result
  1. Understand the issue: inconsistent with related tests, previous values, or the presentation
  2. Pre-analytical explanations: wrong test, patient preparation, sample collection, transport, lab processing error
  3. Analytical explanations: random error, sample mix-up by the lab, methodology difference
  4. Post-analytical explanations: transcription error, patient mix-up in reporting, inappropriate reference interval
  5. Consult a lab professional: explanation, other investigations or alternate methods
  6. Consider additional testing: repeat, different analytical method; Choosing Wisely
  7. Consider that the result could be correct

Homeostatic response to dehydration
  1. Restore osmolality: hypothalamus ↑ osmoreceptor activity, ↓ stretch receptor activity → releases ADH
  2. Conserve fluid: kidneys ↑ water permeability and ↓ urine output → ↑ water reabsorption, prevent further loss
  3. Restore fluid volume: hypothalamus ↑ thirst
  4. Increase BP

Mechanisms involved: secretion of ADH, behavioural changes, changes in sodium balance, cardiovascular reflexes.

lectures.name: Social Determinants of Health and Health Equity
lectures.title: Social Determinants of Health, Health Equity and Critical Appraisal
lectures.framing: Income predicts health in Canada at every stage of the patient pathway. Equity, not equality, is the goal: treat like cases alike (horizontal) and unlike cases differently (vertical). The lecture closes with how to appraise a screening study.
lectures.keypoints: Healthy life expectancy: poorest fifth 50.2 years vs richest fifth 61.4. Health disparity costs Canada $6.1 billion. Horizontal equity = equal treatment of equals; vertical equity = unequal treatment of unequals. In screening studies, lead-time bias and length bias both make screening look better at prolonging survival than it is.

blocks.html:
The income gradient in Canada
  • Life expectancy in full health: poorest fifth 50.2 years; richest fifth 61.4 years
  • Poorest fifth: less use of cancer screening, fewer specialist visits, longer waits, more emergency hospitalizations, more avoidable deaths
  • Income gaps in self-rated mental health and COPD hospitalization have widened over time
  • Cost of health disparity in Canada = $6.1 billion
  • COVID-19 hit marginalized groups disproportionately: chronic multimorbidity, multigenerational/dense households, ability to work from home or self-isolate, testing rates
Equity
  • Horizontal equity: equal treatment of equals in relevant respects
  • Vertical equity: unequal treatment for those who are unequal in relevant respects
Inequalities at key stages of the patient pathway

blocks.cap: Seven points where inequality can be measured between home, primary care, hospital and death: primary care supply and quality, hospital waits, preventable and repeat hospitalisation, dying in hospital, amenable mortality.

blocks.html:
Critical appraisal of a screening study
  • Applying rules of evidence to an original clinical study to decide whether its conclusions are valid and useful
  • How was the study designed? Which screening strategies were compared; were the groups similar at the start?
  • What are the results? Benefits (↓ disease-specific mortality) and potential harms
  • Will the results help me care for my patients? Inclusion/exclusion criteria, results in specific subgroups, whether the technology has changed since publication

rows: Screening detects disease earlier than clinical diagnosis would; if the asymptomatic lag is ignored in survival analysis, survival looks longer even if death is not delayed
Screening disproportionately finds slowly progressing asymptomatic cases, while fast-progressing cases present with symptoms; survival in the screened group is overestimated

lectures.name: Adult Screening and Preventative Care Principles
lectures.title: Adult Screening Tools; Cell Adaptation, Injury and Inflammation
lectures.framing: Two halves: the validated questionnaires used to screen for anxiety, depression and substance use, and the cell's responses to stress: adapt if it can, suffer reversible injury if mildly hit, die by necrosis or apoptosis if not, with inflammation as the host's reaction.
lectures.keypoints: GAD-7 ≥ 11 and PHQ-9 ≥ 10 are the thresholds where action starts. CAGE ≥ 2 = high suspicion, 4 = virtually diagnostic. A mental disorder needs duration and interference/distress; an expectable response to a stressor is not one. Permanent cells cannot undergo hyperplasia. Necrosis always inflames; apoptosis does not. Inflammation runs the 5 Rs: recognition, recruitment, removal, regulation, resolution.

blocks.html:
Definition of a mental disorder
  • A syndrome of clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotion regulation or behaviour, reflecting a dysfunction in the psychological, biological or developmental processes underlying mental functioning
  • Key: the duration of symptoms and the level of interference/distress in social, occupational or other activities
  • An expectable or culturally approved response to a common stressor or loss is NOT a mental disorder
  • Socially deviant behaviour (political, religious, sexual) and conflicts primarily between the individual and society are NOT mental disorders unless they result from a dysfunction in the individual
Normal cell homeostasis

blocks.html:
The inflammatory response
  • Host response to cell/tissue damage and infection: protective and essential for survival
  • Coordinated by inflammatory cells and by cytokines and other mediators
  • Often causes local tissue damage, which should resolve when the response ends
  • Harmful consequences: autoimmune disease (misdirected at self-antigens), allergy (exaggerated against harmless environmental agents), anaphylaxis (uncontrolled)
  • Cardinal signs (Celsus): rubor = redness, calor = heat, dolor = pain, tumor = swelling; plus functio laesa = loss of function (Virchow)
  • Tumor is usually protein-rich fluid leaking into tissue, but may be an abscess (pus)
  • Termination: mediators are made only while the stimulus persists, have short half-lives and are degraded after release; neutrophils die by apoptosis; inflammation itself triggers termination signals

lectures.name: Approach to Neoplasia
lectures.title: Neoplasia Terminology
lectures.framing: The vocabulary of a growth, ordered as a progression: mass → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive malignancy → metastasis. The line that separates pre-malignant from malignant is the basement membrane.
lectures.keypoints: Dysplasia is only visible under a microscope. Carcinoma in situ (high-grade dysplasia) spans the full epithelial thickness but the basement membrane is intact. Malignant = through the basement membrane. A mass or tumour can be benign or malignant; describe it by size, shape, surface/borders, colour and consistency.

blocks.html:
• Mass: abnormal tissue that takes up space as it grows; benign or malignant
    Describe by: size, shape, surface/borders, colour, consistency
  • Tumour / neoplasm: abnormal mass from excessive cell division and evasion of apoptosis; benign or malignant
  • Dysplasia (pre-malignant): dysfunctional growth/maturation and nuclear changes; only seen under a microscope
  • Carcinoma in situ / high-grade dysplasia (pre-malignant): dysplastic cells involve the entire epithelial thickness and push against an intact basement membrane
  • Malignant neoplasm: dysplastic cells have broken through the basement membrane
  • Metastasis: the process and outcome of cancer cells spreading to and invading other tissues

blocks.cap: Dysplasia deepens from mild to severe within the epithelium; carcinoma in situ fills the full thickness above an intact basement membrane; invasive cancer breaks through it.

lectures.name: Cancer Genetics
lectures.title: Cancer Genetics and Oncology Foundations
lectures.framing: A survey of cancer from cell to clinic: what makes a cell malignant (hallmarks, oncogenes vs tumour suppressors, multi-hit carcinogenesis), how cancer is staged, graded, reported and treated, and when to suspect a hereditary syndrome. The organising idea is that cancer is a cascade of mutations, which is why most are sporadic and a minority are inherited.
lectures.keypoints: Oncogenes = gain of function, one hit (Ras, c-myc, HER2, RET); tumour suppressors = loss of function, two hits (p53, Rb, PTEN, BRCA1/2). Stage = size and spread (TNM); grade = how the cells look. Sporadic 70-85%, familial 10-20%, hereditary 5-10%. Red flags for hereditary cancer: early onset, multiple primaries, several affected relatives on one side, a typical pattern, Ashkenazi ancestry. Test an affected relative first; do not test children for adult-onset conditions. CML: t(9;22) BCR-ABL1 → imatinib.

blocks.html:
Carcinogenesis
  • A multi-step process: genetic alterations in DNA controlling the hallmarks lead to malignant transformation; it rarely progresses far enough to become clinically detectable
  • Cancer is rarely one mutation; usually a cascade of successive mutations that destabilize the cell
  • Two-hit hypothesis: normal cell = 2 undamaged chromosomes; 1st hit = hereditary OR a rare event; 2nd hit = cancer
Two-stage clonal expansion model
  1. Initiation: a genetic alteration makes a premalignant cell from a healthy one
  2. Promotion: premalignant cells proliferate
  3. Transformation: a second rapid alteration makes a malignant cell from the premalignant pool
  4. Progression: from the malignant cell to clinical cancer

  • Stage = size and how far it has spread; grade = what the cells look like under a microscope

blocks.html:
Recognizing hereditary cancer
  • Take at least 3 generations on both sides: cancer types, age at diagnosis, new primary vs metastatic, updates
  1. Early-onset cancer: breast < 50, ovarian < 60
  2. Multiple primaries in one person: bilateral breast; breast and ovarian
  3. Multiple affected relatives over several generations on the same side
  4. Overall pattern or types of cancer in the family
  5. Ethnic background: BRCA1/2 in the Ashkenazi Jewish population

HBOC surveillance and risk reduction
  • Breast (women): annual mammogram from age 30, breast MRI age 30-69, prophylactic mastectomy/reconstruction
  • Ovarian: prophylactic surgery at age 35 for BRCA1, age 40 for BRCA2; oral contraceptive use for women > 20
  • Men: clinical breast exam every 6-12 months, annual DRE from 45, annual PSA from 45, annual PEx

Genetic counselling and testing
  • Refer if: personal/FHx of cancer, a test is available and can be interpreted, results may change management, and the patient wants the information
  • Counselling reviews: medical/FHx, likelihood of a syndrome, genes/chromosomes/inheritance, risk of carrying a mutation and of developing cancer, surveillance/risk-reduction options, psychosocial risk
  • Benefits: better understanding and prediction of risk, relief of anxiety/uncertainty, risk management, option of testing for relatives, earlier detection
  • Drawbacks: false positives/negatives; tests cannot find every inherited change; effective risk reduction may not exist; not all relatives want to know; a positive result can bring more worry, visits, tests and procedures
  • Test an affected family member first to confirm the mutation before testing unaffected relatives
  • Avoid testing children for adult-onset conditions: stigmatization, ↑ anxiety, "vulnerable child" parenting

  • Setting: privacy, involve significant others, sit down, look attentive and calm, listening mode, be available
  • Perception: before you tell, ask; if the patient is in denial, do not confront it at the first interview
  • Invitation: obtain overt permission, respecting the right to know (or not to know)
  • Knowledge: give a warning, avoid jargon, use the patient's language, small chunks
  • Empathy: listen for and identify emotions and their source; acknowledge them as they arise

lectures.name: Diagnostic Pathway for Breast Mass
lectures.title: Diagnostic Pathway: Breast Masses
lectures.framing: The same stable → Hx → PEx → Ix → DDx sequence as any workup, applied to a breast lump. The organising idea is imaging chosen by purpose: ultrasound first for a palpable lump or a woman under 30, mammography for screening/diagnosis, MRI for high-risk screening and local staging, CT only for staging after biopsy.
lectures.keypoints: Check for oncologic emergencies first (febrile neutropenia, cord compression, SVC obstruction, hypercalcemia, tumour lysis...). Ultrasound is first-line for a palpable lump and for women < 30. CT is NOT used in workup or screening. No blood or urine test helps diagnose a breast mass; tissue comes from FNAP (≥ 22 G, superficial) or NCB (≤ 21 G, deeper). Cysts and fibroadenomas are well circumscribed; fibrocystic change varies with the cycle.

2. Hx: risk factors

  • What: size, shape, contours, consistency, mobility
  • Nipple, skin, axilla/neck (lymph nodes), other breast/axilla

lectures.name: Communication of the Pathology Report
lectures.title: Physician-Physician Communication of the Pathology Report
lectures.framing: A pathology result is only as good as the information exchanged around it: what the requisition must carry, how the narrative report grades certainty, and when to pick up the phone instead of relying on paper.
lectures.keypoints: The requisition needs clinical information (Hx/imaging, reason, DDx, pitfalls, ancillary tests) and ischemic/formalin times. The narrative report runs from positive → suspicious → atypia (cannot exclude malignancy) → atypia (favour reactive) → negative. Talk directly when the result is unusual, non-concordant, incomplete, rare or urgent.

lectures.name: Healthy Aging vs. Disease
lectures.title: Healthy Aging vs. Disease
lectures.framing: The core skill in geriatrics is separating age-related change (universal, gradual) from disease-related change (not universal). Everything else follows: the older-adult PHE (ALBUS), age-appropriate screening, and recognizing that disease often presents atypically.
lectures.keypoints: Homeostenosis = age-related decline in homeostatic reserve. Older adults get diastolic dysfunction, orthostatic hypotension, ↓ thirst, afebrile infections. ALBUS: Acute issues, Labs/vitals, Book follow-up, Update CPP, Screening (geriatric giants). Disease presents atypically: MI as delirium or functional decline, hyperthyroidism as apathy and new AF, depression without sadness.

blocks.html:
Definitions
  • Ageism: negative or positive stereotypes, prejudice and/or discrimination on the grounds of age
  • Healthy aging: lifelong process of optimizing opportunities to improve and preserve health, physical/social/mental wellness, independence and quality of life, and to enhance life-course transitions

  • Centenarian: lived to or past 100; 1/10 000, 5 F : 1 M
    Associated with: lean males, never-smokers, women who naturally have a child after 40, a 1st-degree relative who reached very old age, low neuroticism/high extraversion, longevity genes
  • Super-centenarian: lived to or past 110
  • Life span: maximum obtainable age for a species, set by the oldest living individual: 122 years in humans
  • Life expectancy: average years a person can expect to live, based on year of birth and current age

lectures.name: Periodic Health Encounter for Older Adults
Mental Health Through Aging (& Depression in Older Adults)
lectures.title: Mental Health Through Aging and Depression in Older Adults
lectures.framing: Most older adults stay emotionally well, helped by stable personality, emotional control and social ties. When depression does occur it hides: less sadness, more somatic and cognitive complaints, and a higher, more lethal suicide rate. The cognitive spectrum is sorted by three questions: subjective change, objective change, functional change.
lectures.keypoints: Screen everyone > 60 and every new LTC admission for depression (PHQ-2 cut-off 3, PHQ-9 cut-off 10, GDS, Cornell in dementia). Suicide is ~2× more frequent and more lethal in older adults; severity of depression is the strongest predictor of suicidal ideation. SIG-E-CAPS. MCI converts to dementia at 10%/year (vs 1-3%). Dementia = cognitive decline that impairs independence in ADLs/IADLs, not only during delirium.

blocks.html:
Mental health through aging
  • Mental disorders are as common in the elderly as in younger groups, except dementing disorders and delirium
  • Prevalence of MDD, anxiety disorders, substance abuse and psychotic disorders is lower over 65
  • Emotional control model: ↑ ability to inhibit negative emotional states and maintain positive ones
  • Personality traits remain stable across the life span
  • Passive coping: reduce emotional distress rather than solve the problem; modify goals, adapt to losses/stressors
  • Strong social ties → better outcomes than isolation or perceived lack of support
  • Resilience: maintaining adaptive behaviour and positive emotion under stress, and recovering from adversity
  • Selective optimization: accommodative rescaling of goals to match one's limitations and the environment's demands

blocks.html:
Depression in older adults
  • Older adults often deny depressed mood and minimize symptoms
  • Cognitive impairment is often associated with depressive symptoms
  • Precipitants: recent bereavement, financial crisis, social isolation
  • Depression is a risk factor for diabetes; dementia and depression are risk factors for each other
  • Hard to recognize because of different clinical features, misperceptions of aging, stigma, coexisting medical illness, anxiety, cognitive impairment, cultural factors
  • Presentation: affective symptoms, cognitive changes, no sadness, lack of feeling/emotion, somatic complaints, irritability, social withdrawal/avoidance, loss of interest/pleasure, unexplained functional decline
  • SIG-E-CAPS: Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicidal ideation
Screening
  • All individuals > 60 and those recently admitted to LTC
  • PHQ-2 (cut-off 3), PHQ-9 (cut-off 10), Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15, GDS-30; yes/no), Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia (19 items; 0 absent, 1 mild/intermittent, 2 severe)

blocks.title: Suicide risk in older adults
blocks.html: Suicide is almost twice as frequent as in the general population and more lethal. Risk factors: white male, 65+, living alone/poor supports, prior attempts, Hx of depression, psychotic features, alcoholism, physical illness, disability, chronic pain, recent loss/bereavement. Severity of depression is the strongest predictor of the course of suicidal ideation.

  2. Is there an objective change? (abnormal cognitive testing)

lectures.framing: A geriatric assessment widens the usual history to what decides outcomes in older adults: medications, function, supports and what matters most. The Geriatric 5Ms are the frame; the high-risk drug list and the geriatric Choosing Wisely items are the commonest ways care goes wrong.

High-risk drugs: opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, beta-blockers, antipsychotics, most of which cause falls. ADLs = DEATH, IADLs = SHAFT. Get collateral when cognition, communication or insight are impaired. Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria, use benzodiazepines first for insomnia/delirium, place feeding tubes in advanced dementia, or chase HbA1c < 7.5% with hypoglycemic drugs.

blocks.html:
Medication adherence
  • Why patients don't take medications as prescribed: complicated regimen, cost, not understanding the benefit or the risk of stopping, side effects, cognitive impairment, disinterest, physical limitations, polypharmacy
  • What the physician can do: explore the reasons; simplify the schedule; use one drug for more than one illness where possible; switch to a cheaper drug or one with fewer side effects; educate on the reason for the drug; consider medication aids; assess cognition; ask a pharmacist to review medications one-on-one

Geriatric Choosing Wisely
  1. Don't use antimicrobials for bacteriuria unless specific urinary tract symptoms are present
  2. Don't use benzodiazepines or other sedative-hypnotics as first choice for insomnia, agitation or delirium
  3. Don't recommend percutaneous feeding tubes in advanced dementia; offer oral feeding
  4. Don't use antipsychotics as first choice for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia
  5. Avoid drugs that cause hypoglycemia to reach HbA1c < 7.5% in many adults 65+; moderate control is generally better

lectures.name: Introduction to Cognitive Testing
lectures.title: Introduction to Cognitive Testing: the 3 Ds
lectures.framing: A cognitive change in an older adult is depression, dementia or delirium until proven otherwise, and the three are told apart mainly by onset, course, attention and level of consciousness. Screening tools, mimic work-up and neuroimaging criteria follow from that.
lectures.keypoints: Delirium = acute, fluctuating, inattentive, altered consciousness, often reversible; do not use MoCA (use 4-AT). Dementia = insidious, chronic, irreversible, attention normal until late. MoCA < 26 and MMSE < 24 suggest impairment; MoCA is better for MCI/mild dementia; RUDAS is less culturally biased. Rule out mimics with CBC, TSH, lytes, Ca + albumin, glucose, B12. Image by BRAIN; CT first. BPSD: DICE, antipsychotics last.

blocks.html:
The 3 Ds of cognitive change
  • Depression: can present with cognitive change, especially in attention, alongside other SIG-E-CAPS symptoms
  • Dementia: umbrella term for diseases causing progressive worsening of cognition
  • Delirium: acute, fluctuating change in cognition and attention that has triggers and may be reversible

DSM-5: major depressive disorder

≥ 5 symptoms in the same 2-week period, including depressed mood or loss of interest:

  • Depressed mood
  • Loss of interest or pleasure in almost all activities
  • Significant unintentional weight loss/gain or ↓/↑ appetite
  • Sleep disturbance (insomnia, hypersomnia)
  • Psychomotor agitation or slowing observable by others
  • Tiredness, fatigue, low energy, or ↓ efficiency at routine tasks

  • Impaired ability to think, concentrate or decide
  • Recurrent thoughts of death (not just fear of dying), suicidal ideation or attempt
DSM-5: dementia (major neurocognitive disorder)
  • Significant decline from previous performance in ≥ 1 domain: learning/memory, language, executive function, complex attention, perceptual-motor, social cognition

  • Not exclusively in the context of delirium
  • Not better explained by another mental disorder
DSM-5: delirium

  • Develops over hours to a few days, is a change from baseline, and fluctuates during the day
  • An additional disturbance in cognition: memory, disorientation, language, visuospatial ability, perception
  • Not explained by a pre-existing neurocognitive disorder; not in the context of severely reduced arousal (coma)
  • Evidence it is a direct physiological consequence of a medical condition, intoxication, withdrawal, toxin, or multiple etiologies

lectures.name: Introduction to Delirium
lectures.title: Delirium
lectures.framing: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention with a precipitant to find (DIMESPPP). The 4-AT screens for it at the bedside, and it matters because it lengthens stays, accelerates decline and raises mortality.
lectures.keypoints: Precipitants: DIMESPPP: Drugs, Infection, Metabolic, Environmental, Structural, Pee, Poo, Pain. 4-AT ≥ 4 = possible delirium; 1-3 = possible cognitive impairment. Acute change/fluctuation and clearly abnormal alertness each score 4 on their own. Delirium ↑ length of stay, long-term cognitive and functional decline, institutionalization, falls, dementia and death.

blocks.html:
Precipitating factors: DIMESPPP

  • Infection
  • Metabolic: hypo-/hypernatremia, hypo-/hypercalcemia, hyperglycemia
  • Environmental
  • Structural: CNS events
  • Pee: UTI, urinary retention
  • Poo: constipation, impaction
  • Pain: uncontrolled, or its medication

lectures.name: Frailty and Falls
lectures.title: Frailty and Falls
lectures.framing: Frailty is lost physiological reserve, not the same as age, comorbidity or disability, and it is graded on the Clinical Frailty Scale. Its commonest consequence is the fall, which is almost always multifactorial. The ICF model describes how a condition becomes a disability.
lectures.keypoints: Frailty = ↓ reserve and resistance to stressors, ↑ vulnerability; not synonymous with comorbidity, disability or aging. CFS runs 1 very fit to 9 terminally ill; 7 = completely dependent but stable, 8 = could not recover from minor illness. Falls: leading cause of injury and 5th leading cause of death over 65. Never call a fall "mechanical": look for intrinsic and extrinsic causes. Prevent frailty with exercise, mobility, Mediterranean diet, protein, and a comprehensive geriatric assessment.

blocks.html:

  • Not synonymous with comorbidity, disability or aging
  • Clinical Frailty Scale: the degree of frailty corresponds to the degree of dementia

International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF)
  • Disability: the interaction between a person's health condition and personal and environmental factors
  • Impairments: problems in body function or structure (e.g. paralysis)
  • Activity limitations: difficulty executing activities (e.g. walking, eating)
  • Participation restrictions: problems with involvement in any area of life (e.g. discrimination in employment or transportation)

blocks.cap: ICF model: a health condition affects body function/structure, activities and participation, which all interact with each other and with environmental and personal factors.

lectures.name: Interdisciplinary Teams & Community Resources for Older Adults

lectures.framing: Two halves: who on the team does what for an older adult (and which local programs to refer to), then the neuroanatomy needed to localize weakness. The organising neuro idea: decide UMN vs LMN from the exam, localize by pattern, then use the tempo of onset to generate the DDx.
lectures.keypoints: UMN (brain, brainstem, cord): brisk reflexes, Babinski, spasticity, no atrophy. LMN (anterior horn to muscle): ↓ reflexes, atrophy, fasciculations. Cerebellar and basal ganglia lesions do NOT cause weakness. Motor fibres decussate in the medullary pyramids; dorsal columns cross in the medulla, spinothalamic fibres cross at cord entry. Cord ends at L1. Hyperacute onset = stroke until proven otherwise; chronic = degenerative/hereditary.

lectures.name: Introduction to Basic and Clinical Pharmacology
Principles of Clinical Pharmacology
lectures.title: Principles of Clinical Pharmacology
lectures.framing: Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body (receptors, agonists/antagonists, potency vs efficacy); pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion). The organising idea: concentration at the site of action, not dose, is what relates to effect.
lectures.keypoints: Lower EC50 = more potent; Emax = efficacy. Competitive antagonists ↓ potency, not efficacy; non-competitive ↓ efficacy, not potency. Partial agonists act as antagonists in the presence of a full agonist. Enzyme induction → lower drug levels, inhibition → higher (reverse for prodrugs); CYP3A4/5 handles ~30%. Half-life ↑ with Vd and ↓ with clearance; steady state and washout both take 3-5 half-lives, independent of dose. A loading dose reaches therapeutic levels faster; narrow therapeutic window = titrate.

blocks.html:
Definitions
  • Pharmacology: the biology, chemistry and physiology of drug disposition, effects and toxicity
  • Drug: a medicine or other substance with a physiological effect when introduced into the body; used to diagnose, treat or prevent disease, or as a component of a medication
  • Clinical pharmacology: study of drug action in humans; the scientific basis for rational, safe, effective prescribing
  • Therapeutics: use of treatments to cure, control or prevent disease
  • Prescribing: a written order saying what medicine is given to whom, in what formulation and dose, by what route, when, how often and for how long
  • Pharmacodynamics: the effects of a drug on the body (how drugs work)
  • Pharmacokinetics: quantitative description of drug concentrations in the body over time (how the body handles drugs)

blocks.cap: PK covers the path from dose to concentration at the site of action (input, distribution, elimination); PD covers the path from that concentration to effect, toxicity and effectiveness.

blocks.html:
• Therapeutic and toxic effects are related to dose, often to the concentration achieved in the blood or tissues affected, and can relate to how long the drug persists there
  • Concentration at the site of action relates to drug effect better than dose

blocks.html:
Pharmacological targets
  • Receptors: ligand-gated ion channels, GPCRs, enzyme-linked receptors, intracellular receptors
  • Enzymes: reductases, transferases, lyases, hydrolases
  • Endogenous molecules: HCl, RANKL, nucleic acids, structural proteins
  • Transport proteins: SGLT2, Na+/K+ ATPase
Receptors
  • Receptor: a macromolecule a drug binds to produce a measurable effect
  • Coupling of the ligand-receptor complex to downstream effectors triggers a signalling cascade
  • Drug-receptor interaction sets the quantitative dose-effect relation and the selectivity of drug action
  • Orthosteric site = main agonist binding site; allosteric sites = other binding sites
  • Receptors exist in active and inactive states; effect ∝ fraction of receptors in the active state
  • Termination: dissociation/destruction of the D-R complex, or receptor desensitization (tolerance, tachyphylaxis)

rows: Changes in membrane potential or intracellular ion concentration

blocks.html:
Dose-response, potency and efficacy
  • Dose-response is closely related to drug-receptor binding
  • Doubling the dose ≠ doubling the effect
  • Drugs have different dose-response profiles; individual variability means you monitor the therapeutic response
  • Efficacy (Emax): maximal response; response rises as receptors are occupied up to Emax, which may occur with all or only a fraction of receptors bound
  • Potency (EC50/ED50): concentration or dose producing 50% of Emax; lower EC50 = more potent
  • Competitive antagonists ↓ potency of agonists but do not change efficacy
  • Non-competitive antagonists ↓ efficacy of agonists but do not change potency

blocks.cap: The response rises steeply then plateaus at Emax, which is why doubling the dose does not double the effect.

blocks.html:
Absorption
  • Absorption: movement of a drug from its site of administration to the systemic circulation
  • Rate of absorption sets onset of action: physicochemical properties/formulation (dissolution, pH, lipid solubility), blood flow, transport proteins (OATs, P-glycoprotein), route (therapeutic goal)
  • Amount absorbed sets magnitude of effect
  • Bioavailability: proportion of administered parent drug reaching the systemic circulation unaltered; depends on absorption (drug properties, DDI, DFI) and the first-pass effect

rows: Convenient (easy to give, dose, transport, store), safe, inexpensive, painless, no infection risk
Poorly soluble drugs, peptides, antibody therapy

Limited absorption, first-pass effect, slower onset, compliance

Needs a health professional, irreversible, costlier, invasive, infection and fluid overload risk
Drug goes straight to the heart: nitric oxide for angina
Useful if unconscious/vomiting; a good fraction of absorbed drug bypasses the portal circulation/liver
Excellent for local action with ↓ systemic exposure

blocks.html: • Route matters for: children (may be unable to swallow a pill), unconscious patients or those unable to swallow (vomiting), mobility issues (may need to sit upright), and when compliance is life-critical (chronic conditions)

Distribution
  • Distribution: movement of drug from the main circulation to its sites of action
  • Highly vascular tissues first (brain, heart, liver, kidneys) → then skin, muscle, fat, bone
  • Blood-brain barrier: highly selective semipermeable barrier restricting many molecules; entry by carrier-mediated transport or lipid solubility
  • Volume of distribution (Vd): extent to which a drug partitions between plasma and tissue compartments
  • Factors: blood flow, capillary permeability, lipid solubility, disease (heart/liver/kidney failure), age (↑ body fat, ↓ plasma volume, ↓ total body water, ↓ extracellular fluid)
Metabolism
  • Metabolism: chemical modification of a drug by a biological system
  • Sites: liver (primary), intestine (enterocytes), stomach (alcohol), kidney, intestinal bacteria
  • Can activate a prodrug, inactivate a drug, ↑ or ↓ toxicity, ↑ effectiveness

blocks.cap: Phase I (ER) makes a lipophilic drug polar by oxidation, reduction or hydrolysis; phase II (cytosol) conjugates it into a water-soluble, usually inactive product. Some drugs enter phase II directly.

blocks.html:
• Phase I: cytochrome P450 mediates most oxidation/reduction; significant genetic variability. CYP3A4/5 30.2%, CYP2D6 20%, CYP2C9 12.8%, CYP1A2 8.9%
  • Phase II: transferases add hydrophilic groups: glucuronidation, acetylation, sulfation, glutathione/thiol conjugation
  • Enzyme induction = LOWER drug levels; enzyme inhibition = HIGHER drug levels; opposite for prodrugs
  • ↑ metabolic rate → ↓ duration/intensity; ↓ metabolic rate → ↑ duration/intensity
  • Factors: DDIs (induction/inhibition), disease (liver/kidney disease, infection, inflammation), age, gender, genetic polymorphisms, blood flow

Excretion
  • Excretion: elimination of parent drug and metabolites from the body
  • Renal: glomerular filtration → passive tubular reabsorption → active tubular secretion → excretion
  • Hepatic metabolism: CYP enzymes
  • Biliary: liver → gallbladder → bile duct → duodenum → feces, OR deconjugated and reabsorbed via the hepatic portal vein (enterohepatic recycling); favours high molecular weight, conjugated, amphipathic molecules
  • Other routes: lungs, sweat, salivary glands, breast milk
  • Clearance (CL): rate of removal from plasma ÷ plasma concentration (mL/min)
  • Factors: drug properties (water solubility), blood flow, renal function (GFR), hepatic function, disease, age (↓ renal plasma flow, ↓ GFR, ↓ functional glomeruli)

blocks.html:
Clinical pharmacology
  • Graded dose-response curve = one patient
  • Quantal dose-response curve = a population, all-or-none: ED50 (therapeutic), TD50 (toxic), LD50 (lethal); % of individuals showing the effect vs log dose; the standard dose is the starting point
  • Half-life (t1/2): time for blood concentration to fall by half; drug is essentially removed after 3-5 half-lives; sets duration of action and dosing frequency
  • Larger Vd = longer t1/2; higher clearance = shorter t1/2; independent of dose
  • Steady state (Css): delivery rate = elimination rate; reached in 3-5 half-lives, independent of dose; with the same daily dose, Css is the same but peak-trough fluctuation differs with the interval
  • Maintenance dose: keeps the peak below the toxic concentration and the trough above the minimum effective concentration
  • Loading dose: larger than maintenance; reaches therapeutic concentration faster
  • Therapeutic window: range between the minimum therapeutic/effective dose and the minimum toxic dose
  • Use ED50 as a starting dose when the window is wide; titrate when it is narrow; monitor efficacy and ADRs
  • Design regimens to avoid toxicity or lack of efficacy and, where possible, give convenient intervals to promote compliance

blocks.cap: Single dose: IV peaks immediately then falls (redistribution α phase, elimination β phase); oral has a lag and lower peak. Duration of action = time above the minimal therapeutic concentration.

Repeated dosing reaches steady state after about 5 half-lives whatever the interval; halving the interval (same dose each time) raises the average level toward toxicity, doubling it lets troughs fall below the therapeutic line.

lectures.name: Principles of Adverse Drug Events and Patient Safety
lectures.title: Principles of Adverse Drug Events and Patient Safety
lectures.framing: Separates what goes wrong despite correct use (an adverse drug reaction) from what goes wrong because of a mistake (an error), and classifies ADRs as immunologic vs non-immunologic, predictable vs unpredictable. Interactions (drug, food, disease) are the commonest predictable cause.
lectures.keypoints: ADR = harm at normal doses with the right drug, dose and route; ADE = any drug-related injury, including errors. Near miss = almost happened. Predictable ADRs: side effect, secondary effect, toxicity, DDI, overdose; unpredictable: pseudoallergic, idiosyncratic, intolerance. Altered elimination is the commonest cause of adverse interactions. Grapefruit inhibits CYP3A4 (statin myopathy, for up to 3 days); leafy greens ↓ warfarin effect. Report new-drug or unusual ADEs to Health Canada.

blocks.html:
Definitions
  • Adverse drug reaction (ADR): any noxious, unintended, undesired effect of a drug at doses used in humans for prophylaxis, diagnosis or therapy; something bad happens even with the right drug, dose and route
  • Adverse drug event (ADE): injury from a drug-related medical intervention; includes errors in administration
  • Error: something bad happens because someone/something made a mistake
  • Preventable adverse event: something bad happens that could have been avoided
  • Near miss: something bad almost happened

Hemolytic anemia after primaquine in G6PD deficiency

blocks.html:
Contraindications and reporting
  • Indication: a disorder for which a drug is effective and should be used
  • Contraindication: a disorder for which a drug is harmful and should not be used
  • On therapy: (1) be aware ADEs can occur, (2) monitor for them, (3) understand the course of the disease
  • Inform the patient, family and other providers about an ADE; report to Health Canada for new drugs or unusual events

lectures.name: Individual Variability in Drug Response
lectures.title: Causes of Variable Drug Response
lectures.framing: The same dose does not give the same effect in everyone. Seven sources of variation, genetics, race, sex, age, kidney disease, liver disease and drug interactions, each act through PK (how much drug reaches the target), PD (how the target responds), or both.
lectures.keypoints: CYP2D6 phenotypes range from poor to ultrarapid metabolizers. Warfarin: 16-fold dose variability, set by VKORC1 and CYP2C9; only S-warfarin is active. Reduce doses in the elderly and monitor renal function; older adults are more sensitive to benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, alpha1 blockers and digoxin. Adjust renally cleared drugs by creatinine clearance. Know the classic CYP3A4 inhibitors (azoles, macrolides, protease inhibitors) and inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St John's wort). PD traps: ACEi + K+-sparing diuretic → hyperkalemia; MAOI + cheese/cold medicine → hypertension.

blocks.html:
Genetics
  • Most people carry at least one variant affecting drug effectiveness or harm
  • CYP2D6: multiphasic distribution of metabolizer phenotypes: poor, intermediate, normal, ultrarapid
  • Warfarin: 16-fold dose variability, narrow therapeutic window; R- and S-enantiomers, only S-warfarin is active against its target (VKOR); variation in VKOR sets sensitivity; variation in the metabolizing enzyme (CYP2C9*2, CYP2C9*3)
Race
  • Not entirely genotype; influenced by environment; may be considered in prescribing
  • Warfarin: VKORC1 and CYP2C9 variation; dose African American > Caucasian > Asian
  • Tacrolimus (antirejection): CYP3A5 variation; African Americans need 2× the dose
  • Rosuvastatin: Asians have 2× plasma levels at the same dose; risk of rhabdomyolysis
  • ACE inhibitors: caution as monotherapy in Black Canadians (less effective)
  • BiDil (isosorbide dinitrate + hydralazine): approved for African Americans with congestive heart failure

Kidney disease

Drug-drug interactions

  • PK examples: erythromycin → 2.5-fold ↑ felodipine levels → hypotension admissions; rifampin → 87% ↓ simvastatin levels (↑ synthesis of metabolizing enzymes)
  • PK risk factors: narrow therapeutic window, drugs eliminated by one major pathway, prodrugs, inducer/inhibitor "perpetrators"

lectures.name: Therapeutics Across the Lifespan
lectures.title: Therapeutics Across the Lifespan
lectures.framing: Prescribing changes at both ends of life: older adults bring polypharmacy and prescribing cascades, children bring immature PK and age-specific ADRs. The second half places the prescription in its system: STEPS for choosing a drug, adherence, and how drugs are developed, approved, priced and paid for in Canada.
lectures.keypoints: Polypharmacy = 5-10+ medications; review at least annually and at every transition (bring the bottles). Neonatal GFR is low and reaches adult values at 6-12 months; CYP activity exceeds adult values at 3-6 years. Classic pediatric ADRs: aspirin → Reye, chloramphenicol → grey baby, benzyl alcohol → gasping, sulfonamides → kernicterus, tetracycline → teeth, valproate → liver (< 4 y). STEPS: Safety, Tolerability, Effectiveness, Price, Simplicity. Health Canada approves; PMPRB caps price, CADTH judges value, pCPA negotiates, plans list on formularies. Direct-to-consumer advertising is not legal in Canada.

blocks.html:
Therapeutics in older adults
  • Polypharmacy: use of multiple medications; minimum 5-10
  • More medications = ↑ cost, ADRs, poor adherence, DDIs, hospitalization
  • Factors leading to ADRs: multimorbidity, age-related PK/PD change, prescribing cascades, heterogeneity, exclusion from clinical research, fragmented/specialized care, frequent care transitions, evolving guidelines
  • Review medications at least annually: have patients bring their bottles; review at transitions of care; ask about side effects/benefits; look for duplication and cascades; eliminate unnecessary drugs; simplify regimens
Before starting a new medication, ask
  • Is it necessary? Does it fit the patient's frailty status and goals?
  • Is it covered by the Ontario Drug Benefit? What are the therapeutic endpoints?
  • Do benefits outweigh risks? Am I treating the effect of another drug?
  • Could one drug treat two conditions? Could it interact with diseases or other drugs?
  • Does the patient know what it is for and what to watch for?

Therapeutics in pediatrics
  • Differences in PK/PD and compliance; lack of age-appropriate formulations
  • Subgroups: preterm newborn; term newborn (0-27 d); infant/toddler (28 d-23 mo); child (2-11 y); adolescent (12-16/18 y)

blocks.html:
Canadian health care system and drug therapy
  • Health care was made a provincial responsibility at Confederation (cheap then, few drugs); it has grown to universal coverage of basic health services and hospital care (40-50% of provincial budgets)
  • 10 provincial, 3 territorial and a small federal system (Canadian Armed Forces, federal prisons)

blocks.cap: Federal government funds provinces through the Canada Health Act transfers and directly covers First Nations, Inuit, Forces, veterans, federal inmates and some refugees; provinces deliver care through regional health authorities.

blocks.html:
• Drugs are prescribed by physicians (provincial); paid for by patients, private plans and governments (federal, provincial); approved, regulated and monitored federally; sold by industry (federal regulation, provincial incorporation)
  • Drug formulary: list of medications approved for use in a hospital or covered by a drug plan
  • Every province and territory has a drug plan; number/type of drugs and eligibility vary considerably

blocks.cap: Three layers of coverage: layer one (hospitals, physicians, diagnostics) is fully public; layer two, including prescription drugs, is mixed public/private; layer three (dental, vision, physio) is almost all private.

blocks.html:
Drug utilization in Canada
  • Total drug spending $40 billion/year = 16% of health costs; $1100/person; 85% on prescription drugs
  • Paid 50% public, 25% private plans, 25% individuals
  • Patients ≤ 18 average 4 prescriptions/year; the number rises with age
  • Most prescribed classes: cardiovascular, psychotherapeutics, GI/genitourinary
  • Largest share of sales: antineoplastic/immunomodulating agents, general anti-infectives, alimentary tract/metabolism
  • Major cost drivers: age and high-cost drugs (rheumatoid arthritis/Crohn's disease, hepatitis C, age-related macular degeneration)
  • Pharmaceutical spending per capita: OECD average $719; Canada $1043, #3 after the USA and Switzerland
  • Life expectancy: OECD average 80.6; Canada 81.7 but ranks #13
  • Barriers to optimal drug therapy: finances, SDH, geography, health system access

Drug development and regulation
  • Drugs are approved for sale by the Health Products and Food Branch of Health Canada
  • Therapeutic Products Directorate: drugs
  • Biologic and Genetic Therapies Directorate: vaccines, biologics

Industry and physicians
  • Historically, industry spent considerable effort and money to influence physician behaviour
  • Guidances and codes of conduct now set clear boundaries between physicians and industry representatives
  • In Canada, industry has found marketing to physicians inefficient per sale
  • Direct-to-consumer advertising: a physician is less likely to refuse a patient's suggestion; not legal in Canada
